pack.title: Starter Core: Algorithms, Backend, Systems
pack.description: Three standalone practice lessons for recognising an invariant, defining a retry-safe boundary, and reasoning about recoverable work.

tracks.title: DSA
tracks.description: Practice the pair-sum hash lookup invariant.

tracks.title: Distributed systems
tracks.description: Practice durable intent and recovery after process loss.

sessions.title: Find a pair that reaches the target
sessions.prompt: Given an unsorted list of integers and a target, which strategy finds whether two different positions sum to the target in linear expected time?
options: Sort the list and compare every pair
Keep seen values in a hash map and look up the complement before storing the current value
Use a nested loop and stop after the first match
sessions.feedback: The lookup records values that appeared earlier. For each current value x, target minus x names the only earlier value that can complete the pair.
sessions.model: Maintain the invariant: before processing the current value, the map contains exactly the values from earlier positions. Looking up target minus current decides whether an earlier partner exists without revisiting every pair.
sessions.example: values = [2, 7, 11], target = 9. Before 7, seen is {2}. The needed complement is 2, so the pair is found.
sessions.trigger: The prompt asks for a pair, membership or complement over an unsorted collection.
sessions.nonTrigger: If the input is sorted and pointer movement is available, a two-pointer method may be simpler and use less extra memory.
sessions.invariant: The map contains only earlier values, so a successful lookup names two distinct positions.

trace.note: No earlier partner exists, so store 2.
The complement is already present, so stop with a valid pair.

decision.prompt: Why check the complement before storing the current value?
options: It avoids using the same position twice when target equals twice the value
decision.feedback: Checking first preserves the earlier-position invariant, including duplicate values.

sessions.explainPrompt: Explain the hash lookup invariant, one tempting wrong approach, and the expected time and space costs using a fresh example.
checklist: I stated the invariant and complexity.
rubric: Clarify whether values may repeat and whether positions must differ.
State the brute-force baseline before selecting the invariant.
Run an empty, duplicate, and no-match case.
sessions.reviewPrompt: Why does checking before insertion matter when the target is twice the current value?
sessions.task: In your own editor, implement a method that returns two distinct positions or an explicit no-match result. Record the three cases you actually ran.

sessions.title: Make a retried command safe
sessions.prompt: A client sends a command, loses the response, and retries. Which contract prevents a duplicate side effect?
options: Persist a scoped idempotency key, request fingerprint, and result atomically
Retry until an HTTP 200 response arrives
sessions.feedback: A user-interface control cannot coordinate retries from another process. The command needs durable identity at the write boundary.
sessions.model: A retry repeats an uncertain intention. Scope an idempotency key, bind it to a request fingerprint, and atomically reserve the key with the durable result. The same key and payload replay the result; the same key with a changed payload conflicts.
sessions.example: Command key import-42 is accepted, but the response is lost. Repeating import-42 with the same fingerprint returns the recorded command rather than creating another one.
sessions.trigger: A network response can be lost after a side effect may already have committed.
sessions.nonTrigger: A genuinely new intention needs a new key even if its payload looks similar.
sessions.invariant: At most one accepted result exists for a scoped key and fingerprint.

trace.note: A separate read then insert races with another writer.
A later retry can read durable truth after a process crash.

decision.prompt: Two processes observe an absent key at the same time. What arbitrates the result?
options: A shared uniqueness constraint with a transaction
decision.feedback: Only shared atomic enforcement can decide between concurrent writers.

sessions.explainPrompt: Explain retry, duplicate intention, and conflicting payload. Name the atomic boundary and one remaining crash window.
checklist: I distinguished a retry from a new command.
I named the durable enforcement point.
rubric: Describe duplicate, conflict, and in-progress responses.
Name the transaction or uniqueness boundary.
State what a single-process demonstration cannot prove.
sessions.reviewPrompt: What must a retry read after the original process commits but crashes before replying?
sessions.task: Write a short command contract with key scope, request fingerprint, duplicate response, conflict response, and one concurrency test you would run.

sessions.title: Keep long-running work recoverable
sessions.prompt: A service records a work request successfully, then its enqueue call fails. Which design preserves intent without pretending both systems share one transaction?
options: Discard the request and ask the client to retry
Persist recoverable enqueue intent such as an outbox, then retry delivery
Keep retry state only in process memory
sessions.feedback: Durable intent survives process loss. Delivery can retry later, while workers still need idempotent handling because messages may repeat.
sessions.model: Separate accepting intent from delivering work. A durable record captures what was accepted; a delivery process retries publication; workers make effects safe under duplicate delivery. Recovery is a state machine, not a hope that calls happen once.
sessions.example: A job row and outbox event commit together. The process exits before publication. A later dispatcher reads the outbox and sends the work without losing the accepted job.
sessions.trigger: Two durable systems must coordinate but cannot share an atomic transaction.
sessions.nonTrigger: A synchronous call may be sufficient when the caller can safely fail before any durable intent exists.
sessions.invariant: Every accepted work request remains discoverable until delivery reaches a defined terminal state.

trace.code: accept request -> commit job and outbox
trace.note: The accepted intention is durable before external delivery.
A crash after commit does not erase the delivery obligation.

decision.prompt: Why does the worker still need idempotency after an outbox is added?
options: Publication and delivery can still repeat
The database now controls every dependency
decision.feedback: At-least-once delivery remains possible, so the effect boundary needs its own duplicate protection.

sessions.explainPrompt: Draw accept, durable intent, delivery, worker effect, and recovery. Identify one crash between adjacent steps and how the system responds.
checklist: I named a durable recovery record.
I explained why duplicate delivery remains possible.
rubric: State the terminal states and retry owner.
Trace at least one process-loss scenario.
Separate demonstrated behavior from design intent.
sessions.reviewPrompt: What evidence shows an accepted request was neither silently lost nor applied twice after a restart?
sessions.task: Draw a five-state recovery flow for accepted work. Mark the durable records, retry owner, and one duplicate-delivery defense.
